title: T4 — HCP Terraform concepts
bodyMarkdown:
## HCP Terraform concepts

Exam group **8**. Group 1 (1b) introduced HCP Terraform briefly as a team collaboration tool, and group 6 (6c) introduced the `cloud` block that connects a configuration to HCP Terraform workspaces, plus the fact that the `cloud` block and a `backend` block cannot coexist. This group opens the product itself: how runs execute, which collaboration and governance features it adds, how workspaces and projects organize work, and how the CLI connects to it.

A note on the name. The docs say "Effective April 22, 2024, Terraform Cloud is now HCP Terraform." The product is the same: "HCP Terraform's functionality remains the same." Older study material that says Terraform Cloud means this product, and this lesson uses the current name. Terraform Enterprise is a different offering: "our self-hosted distribution of HCP Terraform."

### tf.004.8a — Use HCP Terraform to create infrastructure

#### Remote runs

HCP Terraform is "an application that helps teams use Terraform together." The central idea is that it runs Terraform for you. "Terraform runs managed by HCP Terraform are called remote operations," and HCP Terraform "can perform Terraform runs on its own disposable virtual machines." That gives a consistent run environment instead of whoever's laptop happens to have the right credentials. HCP Terraform always runs in the context of a workspace, which supplies the configuration, state and variables for the run (8c covers how workspaces are organized). For workspaces with remote operations enabled, which is "the default" for a workspace left on its default settings (a project or organization can set a different default; see 8c), the run happens in HCP Terraform even when you start it from your own terminal. The docs say CLI operations "are remotely executed in HCP Terraform's run environment by default."

The plan and apply split is unchanged: "It always plans first, then uses that plan's output for the apply." By default a person has to approve: "In the default configuration, HCP Terraform waits for user approval before running an apply." A workspace can be set to apply successful plans automatically, and "If a plan contains no changes, HCP Terraform does not attempt to apply it," so the run ends as "Planned and finished". Each run passes through the stages "pending, plan, cost estimation, policy check, apply, and completion" (8b explains cost estimation and policy checks). The cost estimation stage "only occurs if cost estimation is enabled," and the policy check stage "only occurs if Sentinel policies are enabled," so a run without those features skips them. An OPA policy check stage is conditional in the same way: "This stage only occurs if you enabled Open Policy Agent (OPA) policies."

Runs wait in line. 6b mentioned HCP Terraform's queued locking; this is the queue behind it: "Each workspace in HCP Terraform maintains its own queue of runs, and processes those runs in order." A run that is waiting for another to finish sits in a pending state. Plan-only runs are an exception to the queue: they "can proceed at any time and do not block the progress of other runs."

#### Three ways to start a run

HCP Terraform offers three workflows, and the exam asks you to tell them apart.

- **UI/VCS-driven:** "The UI/VCS-driven run workflow, which is the primary mode of operation." The workspace is linked to a branch of a repository, and HCP Terraform "automatically queues a Terraform run whenever new commits are merged to that branch of workspace's linked repository." The first run of a new VCS-driven workspace is manual: "You must manually trigger an initial run in any new VCS-driven workspace."
- **CLI-driven:** "You can start runs with the standard terraform plan and terraform apply commands" and watch them in your terminal while they execute in HCP Terraform. A remote apply from the CLI has a limit: "Remote terraform apply is for workspaces without a linked VCS repository." The docs add "You cannot run remote applies in workspaces that are linked to a VCS repository", because the repository is the source of truth there.
- **API-driven:** "In the API-driven workflow, workspaces are not directly associated with a VCS repo." Your own tooling, such as a CI system, decides when to run and "must upload the configurations as a .tar.gz file." The contrast with VCS-driven is that "HCP Terraform does not fetch configuration files from version control."

Do not mix up what starts a run, which is the workflow, with where it executes, which is the execution mode covered in 8c. The workflows differ in how the configuration arrives and what triggers the run.

#### Speculative plans

A speculative plan is a preview that cannot change anything. "Speculative plans are plan-only runs." They "show possible changes, and policies affected by those changes, but cannot apply any changes." The docs list three ways to start one. In VCS-backed workspaces, "pull requests start speculative plans" and HCP Terraform posts a link to the plan in the pull request. This is conditional: "Pull requests can only trigger runs in workspaces where automatic speculative plans are allowed," and a pull request "will only trigger speculative plans in workspaces that are connected to that pull request's destination branch." With the CLI integration, running `terraform plan` starts one: "terraform plan starts a speculative plan in an HCP Terraform workspace." The runs API "creates speculative plans whenever the specified configuration version is marked as speculative" (a configuration version is one saved version of a workspace's configuration, which a run uses); the docs point to the configuration-versions API for details. One safety rule for pull requests: "HCP Terraform doesn't run speculative plans for pull requests that originate from forks of a repository."

Saved plans are a different thing. `terraform plan -out` followed by `terraform apply` on the saved file works against HCP Terraform too: "Using saved plans from the CLI with HCP Terraform requires at least Terraform CLI v1.6.0." Like remote apply, "remote saved plans are for workspaces without a linked VCS repository."

The discriminator: remote operations run on HCP Terraform's own machines and always plan before apply; VCS-driven runs start from commits, CLI-driven runs start from `terraform plan` and `terraform apply`, API-driven runs start from your own tooling uploading a `.tar.gz`; a speculative plan is plan-only and never applies.

**Exam tip:** "merged commit starts a run and a pull request shows a plan" is VCS-driven; "`terraform apply` in a workspace with no repository runs remotely" is CLI-driven; "CI pipeline uploads a `.tar.gz` configuration" is API-driven; "preview that can never be applied" is a speculative plan; "plan output must be approved before apply by default" is the default confirmation step.

### tf.004.8b — Describe HCP Terraform collaboration and governance features

#### Teams and permissions

Collaboration starts with who may do what. "To control access within organizations, add users to a team and grant the team permissions to perform actions." Team management is a paid feature: "Team management is available in HCP Terraform Essentials, Standard, and Premium editions." The free tier is for small teams: "Small teams can sign up for free to connect Terraform to version control, share variables" and store state remotely. In contrast, "Paid editions allow you to add more than five users, create teams with different levels of permissions" and more. "Every organization has an owners team."

Permissions can be set at organization, project and workspace scope, and they add up: "Each permission is additive, granting a user the highest level of permissions possible, regardless of which scope set that permission." The reverse also holds: the organization-level View all workspaces permission "does not override the Write role set on a specific workspace."

At the workspace level the built-in roles are Read, Plan, Write and Admin, and "Each role builds upon the previous level, with Admin granting the most comprehensive access." The Plan role is for people who "might propose changes to managed infrastructure, but whose proposed changes should be approved before they are applied." The Write role is for people who "do most of the day-to-day work of provisioning and modifying managed infrastructure." The permission that separates them is applying: Apply means "Approve and apply Terraform plans in the workspace," while Plan means "Queue Terraform plans in the workspace." Read means "View information about workspace runs." Settings are admin-only: workspace admins can "Read and write workspace settings, such as general settings, notification configurations, and run triggers."

#### Policy as code and enforcement levels

Governance means rules that a plan must pass. "Policies are rules that HCP Terraform enforces on Terraform runs." Two frameworks matter here:

- **Sentinel:** "Sentinel: HashiCorp's policy-as-code framework." HCP Terraform gives Sentinel policies four imports, described as the ones that "define policy rules for the plan, configuration, state, and run," named `tfplan`, `tfconfig`, `tfstate` and `tfrun`.
- **OPA:** "OPA: Open Policy Agent with Rego language." A policy has a query, and "If the array is empty, HCP Terraform reports that the policy has passed."

The docs list a third framework labeled "Terraform policy (beta)"; this lesson covers Sentinel and OPA. A policy set groups policies and applies them "globally, to specific projects, workspaces" or "to workspaces with specific tags", and "A policy set can only contain policies written in a single policy framework." The same workspace can use several sets in different frameworks. Sentinel and OPA sets do not cover Stacks: "Sentinel and OPA policy sets only support workspaces." The docs also mention Stacks, which are another kind of resource a project can hold next to workspaces ("A project is a folder containing one or more workspaces, Stacks, or both"); this lesson does not cover them. One free-tier limit: "HCP Terraform Free edition includes one policy set of up to five policies." The CLI shows Sentinel results for CLI-driven runs, but "CLI support for policy results is not available for OPA."

#### Enforcement levels

Each policy has an enforcement level that decides what a failure does, and the names differ by framework:

- **Sentinel advisory:** "Failed policies never interrupt the run."
- **Sentinel soft mandatory:** "Failed policies stop the run, but organization admins can configure the platform to allow team members to override failures." The run is paused, and a person with override permission can continue it.
- **Sentinel hard mandatory:** "Failed policies stop the run." Treat it as the level that cannot be overridden by default: only a policy set configured to allow overrides changes that. A policy set has the option "This policy set can be overridden in the event of mandatory failures," which lets users with the appropriate permissions override "any failed policy checks in that set, even policies set to Hard mandatory," and the docs say this setting "takes precedence over the individual policy's enforcement level."
- **OPA:** "OPA provides two policy enforcement levels." They are advisory and mandatory, and for OPA "mandatory: Failed policies stop the run, but any user with Manage Policy Overrides permission can override these failures".

The trap is the word "mandatory". Sentinel has soft and hard mandatory; OPA has one mandatory level, and that one can be overridden by a user with the override permission.

#### Run tasks, cost estimation and health

Run tasks reach outside HCP Terraform: they "let you directly integrate third-party tools and services at certain stages in the HCP Terraform run lifecycle." A task can start at four points:

- "Pre-plan: Before Terraform creates the plan."
- "Post-plan: After Terraform creates the plan."
- "Pre-apply: Before Terraform applies a plan."
- "Post-apply: After Terraform applies a plan."

Tasks have their own enforcement levels, which are not the policy levels above: "Advisory: Run tasks can not block a run from completing." and "Mandatory: Failed run tasks can block a run from completing." With several tasks, "the run ends based on the most restrictive enforcement level in each associated run task." Tasks run in workspaces that use Terraform "1.1.9 and later." Do not confuse run tasks (an external service called by HCP Terraform) with Sentinel or OPA policies (rules evaluated by HCP Terraform itself).

Cost estimation is off until you turn it on: "HCP Terraform disables cost estimation by default." Once enabled, "Estimated costs appear in the run UI as an extra run phase, between the plan and apply." The docs warn that it is only an estimate: "Note that this is just an estimate".

Health assessments check a workspace after it is built. "Drift detection determines whether your real-world infrastructure matches your Terraform configuration," and continuous validation checks conditions that "continue to pass after Terraform provisions the infrastructure." The docs state the plan tiers exactly: "Health assessments are available in HCP Terraform Standard and Premium editions." A workspace needs "Remote execution mode or Agent execution mode for Terraform runs", so a workspace in Local execution mode does not meet the requirement (this follows from the requirement; the docs do not name Local mode). Group 6 covered finding drift by hand with `-refresh-only`; health assessments are the scheduled version, because "HCP Terraform periodically runs health assessments for your workspace."

#### Audit trails and the private registry

Audit trails record who changed what: the events "describe changes to the application entities (workspaces, runs, etc.) that belong to an HCP Terraform organization." The retention window is short: "HCP Terraform retains 14 days of audit log information." They have a tier too: "Audit trails are available in HCP Terraform Standard and Premium editions." Reading them through the API takes a specific credential: "You must access it with an organization token or an audit trail token."

The private registry is the sharing mechanism, which group 1 listed and group 5 used in a source address: it "helps you share Terraform providers and Terraform modules across your organization." Private providers and modules "are only available to members of that organization," and you can write Sentinel policies to control module use: "You can create Sentinel policies to manage how members of your organization can use modules from the private registry."

The discriminator: teams and roles control who may act; Sentinel and OPA policies control what a plan may contain; run tasks call external tools; cost estimation, health assessments and audit trails report on money, drift and activity.

**Exam tip:** "can plan but must not apply" is the Plan role; "soft mandatory" or "hard mandatory" is Sentinel (hard mandatory is overridable only when its policy set allows overrides), and "mandatory" with an override permission is OPA; "external scanner called before apply" is a run task; "alert that infrastructure no longer matches configuration" is drift detection in health assessments; "who changed a workspace last week" is the audit trail; "share approved modules inside the organization" is the private registry.

### tf.004.8c — Describe how to organize and use HCP Terraform workspaces and projects

#### HCP Terraform workspaces are not CLI workspaces

The word "workspace" means two things, and the docs say so directly: "Both HCP Terraform and Terraform CLI have features called workspaces, but they function differently." An HCP Terraform workspace "contains everything Terraform needs to manage a given collection of infrastructure," and HCP Terraform "manages infrastructure collections with workspaces instead of directories." It holds the configuration (from a linked repository or uploaded), the variable values and the state. Each workspace also keeps history: "Each workspace retains backups of its previous state files."

The differences to memorize:

- "HCP Terraform workspaces are required," because "You cannot manage resources in HCP Terraform without creating at least one workspace." They are also a basis for access control, since you grant users and teams permissions on them.
- "Terraform CLI workspaces are associated with a specific working directory and isolate multiple state files in the same working directory." Group 6 (6a) defined that kind. "The Terraform CLI does not require you to create CLI workspaces."

The docs recommend small workspaces: "We recommend that organizations break down large monolithic Terraform configurations into smaller ones." Their example is networking, application and monitoring configurations for production, each with its own workspace so you can "assign separate teams to manage them," which, the docs say, "enables teams to make changes in parallel."

#### Projects

Projects group workspaces. "Projects let you organize your workspaces into groups." Every workspace has exactly one: "Every workspace and Stack must belong to exactly one project." The starting point is the default project: "By default, all workspaces belong to an organization's Default Project," and "You can rename the default project, but you cannot delete it." You can choose a project when you create a workspace and "move it to a different project later."

A project is also a permission boundary. "Each project has a separate permissions set" that grants teams access to all its workspaces, so projects suit business units or technical teams. Tier note, as the docs state it: "Projects are available to all users, but managing project permissions requires HCP Terraform Essentials, Standard, or Premium edition." The "Manage all Projects" permission lets a team manage projects.

#### Execution mode

A workspace decides where its runs execute:

- **Remote:** "HCP Terraform performs Terraform runs on its own disposable virtual machines." The docs list Sentinel policy enforcement, cost estimation and notifications as features of remote execution ("enables advanced features, such as Sentinel policy enforcement, cost estimation, notifications"), and Local mode "disables remote execution."
- **Local:** "Lets you perform Terraform runs on your local workstation using the CLI-driven run workflow." HCP Terraform keeps the state, and "HCP Terraform does not evaluate workspace variables or variable sets in local execution mode." The docs describe it as making the workspace "act only as a remote backend for Terraform state."
- **Agent:** "Lets HCP Terraform communicate with lightweight HCP Terraform agents." Use it "to run Terraform in isolated, private, or on-premises infrastructure." Agents are "a paid feature."

Defaults come in layers, so "Remote" is not one universal default. A workspace's own setting starts as "Project Default: HCP Terraform uses a project's default execution mode to choose the execution platform for a workspace." A project in turn uses the organization's mode unless you override it: "a project uses the organization's execution mode, which is either Remote or Local." Workspaces created in a project after you change its mode "inherit the project default." One place the docs state Remote as the default is a workspace that `terraform init` creates (8d).

#### Variables and variable sets

HCP Terraform keeps two kinds of variable: "You can create both environment variables and Terraform variables in HCP Terraform." Terraform variables are the input variables from group 4; "In workspaces, Terraform variables refer to input variables," and "If a required input variable is missing, Terraform plans in the workspace will fail." Environment variables are shell variables set before the run: "Environment variables can store provider credentials and other data." The docs prefer them for credentials: "We also recommend passing credentials to Terraform as environment variables instead of Terraform variables when possible." In a CLI-driven run, a local `TF_VAR_` variable can feed an input variable, but "you must still set all required environment variables, like provider credentials, inside the workspace."

Marking a variable sensitive is one-way: it "makes it write-only and prevents all users (including you) from viewing its value in the HCP Terraform UI." Group 4 taught that `sensitive` is a display control and not encryption; the HCP Terraform warning agrees: "There are some cases when even sensitive variables are included in logs and state files." And "HCP Terraform stores variable descriptions in plain text," so never put a secret in a description.

Variable sets avoid repeating the same variables: "you can create variable sets to reuse the same variables across multiple workspaces and Stacks" (Stacks are glossed in 8b). They have scopes. A workspace-scoped set applies to "multiple workspaces within the same organization", a project-scoped set is "Automatically applied and available to all current and future workspaces and Stacks within a project", and a global set is "Automatically applied to all current and future workspaces and Stacks within an organization." When keys collide, "Workspace-specific variables always overwrite variables from variable sets that have the same key," and on the command line, `-var` or `-var-file` values "overwrite workspace-specific and variable set variables that have the same key." A variable set can be marked as priority, and that is the exception: "If prioritized, variables in a global variable set have precedence over all other variables with the same key."

#### Run triggers

Workspaces often depend on each other. A **run trigger** connects them: it lets "runs to queue automatically in your workspace on successful apply of runs in any of the source workspaces." Each workspace can have "up to 20 source workspaces," and configuring one "requires admin access to the workspace." A triggered run does not apply by itself: "Runs initiated by a run trigger do not auto-apply unless you enable the Auto-apply run triggers setting."

#### Remote state and workspace locking

To read another workspace's values you use remote state sharing. "A common way to share information between workspaces is the terraform_remote_state data source," which reads a source workspace's outputs (group 4 noted that root module outputs are what it exposes). Sharing is off by default: "By default, new workspaces in HCP Terraform do not allow other workspaces to access their state." You can share with all workspaces in the organization, with all workspaces in the same project ("All other workspaces in the same project can access this workspace's state during runs."), or with specific workspaces. HCP Terraform recommends the `tfe_outputs` data source: "The tfe_outputs data source is more secure because it does not require full access to workspace state to fetch outputs." And "Remote state access controls do not apply when using the tfe_outputs data source."

Do not confuse two kinds of locking. Locking a workspace stops new HCP Terraform runs (plan-only runs are not affected: "Locking does not affect plan-only runs"): "A lock prevents HCP Terraform from performing any applies in the workspace," and "New runs remain in the Pending state until the workspace unlocks." State locking, taught in 6b, is Terraform preventing two operations from writing state at once.

The discriminator: an HCP Terraform workspace is a required unit of configuration, state, variables and permissions, while a CLI workspace is an extra state in a directory; projects group workspaces and carry permissions; execution mode chooses where runs execute; variable sets share variables; run triggers start runs, and remote state sharing exposes outputs.

**Exam tip:** "required, holds its own variables and run history" is an HCP Terraform workspace, and "extra state in the same directory" is a CLI workspace; "group workspaces and set team access for all of them" is a project; "plan and apply on our own machines, HCP Terraform only stores state" is Local execution mode; "private network, no inbound access" is Agent mode; "same credentials in many workspaces" is a variable set; "apply in workspace A should start a run in workspace B" is a run trigger.

### tf.004.8d — Configure and use HCP Terraform integration

#### Logging in

The CLI needs a credential first. "Run terraform login to authenticate with HCP Terraform." The command "obtains an API token," and "If you don't provide an explicit hostname, Terraform will assume you want to log in to HCP Terraform at app.terraform.io." It is interactive: "You can only use this command in interactive scenarios because the command launches a web browser". By default Terraform will "save it in plain text in a local CLI configuration file called credentials.tfrc.json." For automation you configure credentials manually instead. A token can also be written in the `cloud` block, but the docs advise against it: "We recommend omitting the token from the configuration".

#### The cloud block

6c introduced the `cloud` block; here are its arguments. "The cloud block is a member of the terraform block." The first, `organization`, "Specifies the name of an HCP Terraform organization to connect to." Under `workspaces` you choose how to pick workspaces, with exactly one of two selectors:

- **`name`:** a single workspace. "If you configure the name, you cannot use the tags configuration." With `name`, "You can only use the working directory with the workspace named in the configuration," and "You cannot manage the workspace from the Terraform CLI."
- **`tags`:** many workspaces. "Terraform associates the configuration with workspaces that match all tags." "New workspaces created from the working directory inherit the tags."

A third argument, `project`, narrows it: "Terraform creates all workspaces that use this configuration in the project." The `hostname` argument defaults to app.terraform.io and matters for Terraform Enterprise. As 6c said, `cloud` and `backend` are mutually exclusive, and the `terraform` block reference repeats it: "You cannot configure a backend block when the configuration also contains a cloud configuration for storing state data." The block exists in Terraform 1.1 and later: "The cloud block is available in Terraform v1.1 and later."

Environment variables can supply the same settings. The docs say this "is helpful when you want to use the same Terraform configuration in different HCP Terraform organizations and projects." They are `TF_CLOUD_ORGANIZATION` ("The name of the organization."), `TF_CLOUD_PROJECT` and `TF_CLOUD_HOSTNAME`. Terraform uses them only when the argument is missing: "If both are specified, the configuration takes precedence." If you configure everything with them, "you must still add an empty cloud block in your configuration file." `TF_WORKSPACE` selects one workspace, and "HCP Terraform will not create a new workspace from this variable; the workspace must exist in the specified organization."

#### Initializing and migrating state

"After adding or changing a cloud block, run the terraform init command to complete the set up." If the block names a workspace that does not exist yet, "HCP Terraform will create a new workspace with that name when you run terraform init." Check the new workspace in the UI before running anything, because the docs warn that "New workspaces are not automatically connected to a VCS repository and do not have a working directory specified." For a workspace that `terraform init` creates, the docs say the execution mode defaults to Remote, "so that runs occur within HCP Terraform's infrastructure instead of on your workstation."

State moves with `init`, just as 6c showed for other backends. If the directory has existing state, "Terraform prompts you to migrate state from any existing workspaces." "HCP Terraform requires all workspaces to have a name," so "Terraform may also prompt you to rename your workspaces during the migration." CLI workspaces such as production and staging get renamed because HCP Terraform workspace names "must have unique names within the HCP Terraform organization." Migrating from the older `remote` backend is an edit, not a rewrite: swap `backend "remote"` for `cloud`, and "Terraform continues to use the same set of HCP Terraform workspaces." The `prefix` argument has no equivalent: "the cloud block does not support the prefix argument," so use `tags` instead. A CLI-driven run uploads your directory, and you can keep files out: "you can add a .terraformignore file to the directory and specify files that you do not want to upload".

#### VCS integration

Connecting a repository gives you the VCS-driven workflow from 8a. HCP Terraform needs to list repositories, register webhooks and download code, and it "uses the OAuth protocol to authenticate with VCS providers." Webhooks do the monitoring: "HCP Terraform uses webhooks to monitor new commits and pull requests." A workspace "is linked to one branch of a VCS repository and ignores changes to other branches," and "You can specify which files and directories within your repository trigger runs." With a VCS workspace, "The Terraform code for a normal run always comes from version control."

Two more VCS facts. You can restrict who may use a connection: "By default each VCS connection is enabled for all workspaces and Stacks in the organization," and you can limit it to selected projects. VCS also drives the private registry: "Publishing new versions of a private Terraform module is as easy as pushing a tag to the module's repository."

The discriminator: `terraform login` gets the token, the `cloud` block names the organization and selects workspaces by `name` or `tags` (never both), environment variables such as `TF_CLOUD_ORGANIZATION` fill in omitted arguments, `terraform init` connects and migrates state, and a VCS connection makes commits and pull requests start runs.

**Exam tip:** "authenticate the CLI to HCP Terraform" is `terraform login`; "block can connect many workspaces" is `tags`, and "only one workspace" is `name`; "set the organization from the pipeline environment" is `TF_CLOUD_ORGANIZATION`, with an empty `cloud` block if nothing else is set; "existing local state should move to HCP Terraform" is `terraform init`; "code review shows a plan on the pull request" is a VCS connection.

### Warnings

- Do not run `terraform apply` or `terraform destroy` against real cloud credentials in this workbook, and never call `ExecuteTerraformCommand` or `ExecuteTerragruntCommand` from this workbook's tools.
- Do not connect AWS or other cloud credentials to HCP Terraform on a paid path, and do not sign in to HCP Terraform from this workbook's tools. Hands-on work belongs on a no-charge plan that you operate yourself.
- Plan tiers and edition names change. This lesson quotes them as the docs state them (Free, Essentials, Standard, Premium); check HCP Terraform pricing before relying on a feature, and do not treat any price as taught here.
- Marking a variable sensitive hides it in the UI but does not guarantee it stays out of logs and state, and "HCP Terraform stores variable descriptions in plain text."
- A policy failure is a stop sign only at the enforcement level that says so: advisory never stops a run, overrides exist for soft mandatory and OPA mandatory policies, and for hard mandatory only when the policy set allows them, so do not override a failed policy without reading why it failed.
- `terraform login` saves the API token in plain text by default; do not commit `credentials.tfrc.json` or share it.
